edges.description: Reduced DDX17 alters steady-state expression of a set of genes enriched for nervous system development.
Ddx17 knockdown in embryonic mouse cortex delays the radial migration of upper-layer neurons.
Lowering DDX17 shortens axons in mouse cortical neurons and in Xenopus embryos; overexpression lengthens them.
Proposed link: deregulated axon-guidance receptor and ligand genes may underlie the shortened axons. Not tested directly.
Proposed link through the REST/CoREST complex, which regulates neuronal migration and is co-regulated by DDX17. Not tested directly.
Mispositioned neurons are one route by which cortical wiring can be altered; the axonal defect is separable from it.
Shorter, less branched axons reduce terminal innervation of the contralateral cortex.

edges.limitations: Mosaic acute knockdown in a fraction of cortical neurons rather than constitutional heterozygosity, and shRNA approaches can cause off-target migration defects in mouse cortex; the authors call for genetic knockout models to confirm specificity.

evidence.snippet: All 11 patients in our case series had a neurodevelopmental phenotype, whereby intellectual disability, delayed speech and language, and motor delay predominated.

nodes.description: Heterozygous de novo DDX17 variants are predicted to reduce DDX17 dosage or function. Five are predicted loss-of-function (frameshift, canonical splice) and six are missense; five of the six missense changes fall in the conserved helicase core, two within core DEAD-box motifs. Phenotype severity did not differ between missense and truncating variants, so the authors attribute the disorder to haploinsufficiency rather than a dominant-negative or gain-of-function effect. The gene is strongly constrained against loss-of-function variation in population data (gnomAD LOEUF 0.13).

evidence.reference_title: Monoallelic de novo variants in DDX17 cause a neurodevelopmental disorder.
evidence.snippet: There were no substantial differences in phenotype severity between patients harbouring missense variants versus LoF variants, suggesting DDX17 haploinsufficiency causes the observed phenotype.

nodes.description: In Ddx17-knockdown mouse cortex, callosal axons from layer II/III neurons reach the opposite hemisphere but innervate the contralateral cortex much less densely, with a trend to reduced ipsilateral layer V innervation. Heterozygous ddx17 Xenopus tadpoles have normal gross brain structure but a working memory deficit in a Y-maze assay. Together these indicate a defect in neuronal connectivity rather than a structural brain malformation, which fits the largely nonspecific brain imaging in patients.

nodes.description: DDX17 is a multifunctional regulator of gene expression: a transcriptional co-regulator, a spliceosome component that controls alternative splicing, and a cofactor of the Drosha/DGCR8 microprocessor in microRNA biogenesis. During neuronal differentiation it associates with REST, promotes REST binding to a subset of its target promoters, and with DDX5 regulates proneural microRNAs that target the REST complex. Knocking down DDX17 alone in human SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells deregulates 350 genes enriched for nervous system development, including transcription factors (NEUROG2, RARB, MYCN) and axon-guidance receptors and ligands (DCC, EFNB2, PLXNA2, PLXNA4, SEMA6A, SEMA6D, ROBO2, UNC5D). Which of these targets carries the disease is not known.

nodes.description: Reducing DDX17 shortens axons and reduces collateral branches in cultured mouse cortical neurons, and overexpressing human DDX17 lengthens them, so DDX17 is both necessary and sufficient for normal axon elongation in this system. The effect is not explained by neuronal death. Axon outgrowth from the neural tube is also reduced in heterozygous ddx17 Xenopus tropicalis embryos. The authors report that this axonal role is independent of the migration defect.

nodes.description: After in utero electroporation of Ddx17 shRNAs at E15.5, a significant fraction of upper-layer (layer II/III) mouse cortical neurons fail to reach the superficial cortical layers by postnatal day 21, while neuronal polarisation and axon formation are preserved. The authors caution that shRNA strategies can cause off-target migration defects in mouse cortex and that genetic knockout models are needed to confirm specificity.
